catalog_quote: The statements given in (86) below summarize the stress pattern in the three dialects. (86) a. Stress a superheavy final syllable: mawaaʕíid 'appointment/schedule', xabbár < /xabbar-t/ 'I/you told', maħál < /maħall/ 'place', ṣaargéel 'worm', ʕaaʃméeg 'robe', kubáar 'elders', ʔawláad 'children', taaríix 'history/date' b. Otherwise, stress a heavy penultimate: maħáṭṭa 'station', mánzil 'house', dawáana < /dawaanaa/ 'our medicine', manzílna < /manzilnaa/ 'our house' c. Otherwise, stress a heavy antepenultimate if the final is light: máħfaẓa 'wallet', dárdaʃa 'chatting', mánzilu 'his house' d. Otherwise, stress the penultimate or antepenultimate, whichever is separated from the preceding heavy syllable by an even number of syllables or, if there is no preceding heavy syllable, from the left edge of the word: zambálak 'pendulum', ʔiftákar 'he thought', mustáfa < /mustafaa/ 'Mustafa', zúʕama < /zuʕamaa/ 'leaders', ʔáxadar 'green(m.sg.)', ʔáʕagal 'Be reasonable!', jáxabir 'he knows', máħal 'drought', ʃádara 'tree', dáwa < /dawaa/ 'medicine' ... forms like máħfaẓa 'wallet', mánzil 'house', dáwa from /dawaa/ 'medicine', and dawáana from /dawaanaa/ 'our medicine', indicate that word-final heavy syllables of the form CVC and CVV do not attract stress. ... (87) a. Mora Extrametricality ... b. Foot Construction: From left to right, parse the word into moraic trochees. Degenerate feet are forbidden absolutely. c. Word Layer Construction: End Rule Right

sweep_summary: Sudanese Arabic is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title are by Abdel-Khalig Ali and both are primarily about syncope/epenthesis, not stress. Ali 1996 (TWPL 15) was located via the TWPL issue archive, downloaded open, and read: its sec. 4.2.2 (pp. 24-29) quotes Hamid's 1984 descriptive stress rule for Sudanese Colloquial Arabic and replaces it with a moraic-trochee analysis (left-to-right trochees, final mora extrametrical, End Rule Right). Ali 2017 (Benjamins, DOI 10.1075/sal.5.03ali) is paywalled; its Crossref abstract concerns prosodic domains of syllabification and says nothing about stress; low priority because it condenses Ali's 2014 dissertation, which is open, already held by the project, and contains the fullest first-hand stress statement for the language: (86)-(87), pp. 93-96 (final superheavy > heavy penult > heavy antepenult if final light > trochaic default; final CVC/CVV light). That dissertation statement is the best new statement of this search of works with stress in the title. Still unobtained and worth acquiring for a catalog entry: Hamid 1984 (The Phonology of Sudanese Arabic, U. Illinois diss; IDEALS could not be reached by automated download) as the primary descriptive source Ali corrects, and Dickins 2007 (Khartoum Arabic, EALL). Roset 2018 (Darfur Arabic, sec. 2.5 pp. 31-33, held by the project) describes a different variety with partly different rules (stressed final -i pronominal suffix, contrastive stress). new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive, right-oriented (Cairene-type): a final superheavy (CVVC/CVCC) syllable is stressed; otherwise a heavy penult; otherwise a heavy antepenult when the final is light; in all-light stretches stress falls on the penult or antepenult as determined by left-to-right moraic trochees counted from the last heavy syllable or the word's left edge (so trisyllabic all-light words get initial stress, e.g. ša'dara; four-syllable zamba'lak gets penult). Word-final CVC and CVV do not count as heavy (final mora extrametrical). Formally: final-mora extrametricality, L-to-R moraic trochees, End Rule Right. Same facts in Urban Central Sudanese Arabic, Shukriiya and Hamar. Hamid 1984:37 (quoted p. 80) had summarized: stress the only heavy syllable; if several, the rightmost; otherwise the first syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sec. 2.3.2.4 (pp. 100-102): secondary stress falls on heads of non-main feet built by the same algorithm (e.g. ši`dara'tna 'our tree', fu`gara'akun 'your poor'); 'Although secondary stress is not perceived consistently as such, it is detected through its blocking effect on syncope' (fn. 58); Hamid 1984:47-48 also argued for secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 2.3.2.5: in UCSA the 1sg object suffix /-nii/ and possessive /-ii/ always attract (final) stress ([beeti'] 'my house', [laagaani'] 'he met me'), analysed as lexically accented suffixes suspending extrametricality; Shukriiya/Hamar have regular penult stress there. Epenthetic vowels are invisible to stress (fn. 60), which explains apparent anomalies such as passive/measure VII-VIII forms (in-ke'tal) and Hamid's imperfect-prefix cases. Word-final underlying long vowels surface short and unstressed (da'wa < /dawaa/).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = stem plus affixes and clitics ('phonologically independent unit of segmental material with one primary stress', p. 6); examples are citation forms and suffixed words; secondary stress evidence comes from phrase-level syncope.
new_statements.identity_note: Ali 2014 describes 'Urban Central Sudanese Arabic' (UCSA: Khartoum, Omdurman, Khartoum North, Wad Medani, etc., south to Sennar/Kosti) plus the Shukriiya (Butana) and Hamar (W. Kordofan) dialects, and states the stress facts are essentially the same in all three; UCSA is the core referent of suda1236. Hamid 1984 (quoted inside Ali) describes 'Sudanese Colloquial Arabic' = Khartoum/central variety. Roset 2018 describes Darfur Arabic (western Sudan), a distinct westerly variety that Glottolog files under suda1236 but whose stress system (default initial, contrastive final stress on 3SG object forms) differs; do not use Roset as the suda1236 statement.

new_statements.reading: Word stress in Khartoum/Urban Central Sudanese Arabic (and, per Ali, identically in Shukriiya and Hamar) is quantity-sensitive and right-oriented, bounded to the last three syllables: a final superheavy (CVVC, CVCC) is stressed; otherwise a heavy penult (CVC, CVV); otherwise a heavy antepenult when the final is light; otherwise the penult or antepenult chosen by left-to-right moraic-trochee footing with End Rule Right. Word-final CVC and CVV count as light (final-mora extrametricality). The system is the Cairene type but with mora extrametricality, so ma'hfaza where Cairene has mahfa'za (p. 98). Secondary stress is detected only through its blocking of syncope (fn. 58, p. 100). Ali explicitly refutes Hamid's (1984: 37) 'sole/rightmost heavy syllable, else first syllable' rule with non-derived forms like zamba'lak (pp. 80-87).

tone_statements.citation: Dickins, James. 2007. Khartoum Arabic. In K. Versteegh et al. (eds.), Encyclopedia of Arabic Language and Linguistics, vol. 2, 559-571. Leiden: Brill.
tone_statements.quote: Khartoum Arabic also has a high tone, represented here as ↑, and occurring most commonly in running text on 1st person singular pronoun suffixes, e.g. ummi↑ ‘my mother’ l„y↑ ‘to me’. [...] 1st sg. -y↑/-i↑/-ni↑ [...] The only exception is the 1st sg. suffix form -ni↑, which occurs as the object suffix on verbs and participles, and also in fni↑ ‘in me’ [...] Where the suffixes -a 3rd. sg.fem., -um 3rd pl.masc., and [-in 3rd pl.fem.] are preceded by a short vowel, the main stress falls on the syllable immediately preceding the pronoun suffixes (thus ga¬am ‘pen’, but ga¬áma ‘her pen’).
tone_statements.locator: Preprint sec. 2.2 'Syllable structure', last paragraph, p. 3 (tone statement); sec. 3.2 'Possessive/object suffixes', table p. 4 and text p. 5 (-ni↑, fni↑; stress before -a/-um/-in); sec. 3.3/interrogatives p. 5-6 (minu↑, yātu↑). Published version: EALL vol. 2 pp. 559-571 (page correspondence not checked).
tone_statements.summary: A stress-accent Arabic dialect in which the author additionally posits one high tone (↑) lexically attached to a closed set of morphemes (1SG suffixes -y/-i/-ni, some 3SG.F suffix allomorphs, interrogatives minu 'who', yātu 'which'): a restricted morphological tone, not a general lexical tone system; no L tone, no sandhi described.

sources.note: Sec. 2.5 Word stress (pp. 31-33), DARFUR Arabic (different variety): stress on long vowel or V before CC, the last such if several; otherwise first syllable in 2-3 syllable words; verb + 3SG object suffix stresses final vowel (contrastive: 'kassaro 'they broke' vs kassa'ro 'he broke it'); 1SG =i/=ni stressed; loanwords keep source stress; a-final non-verbs vary.

sources.quote: This paper proposes a prosodic account of syncope and of epenthesis and consonant deletion, which function as strategies for repairing unsyllabified segments, in three dialects of Sudanese Arabic. The analysis identifies the precise prosodic domains of syllabification in these dialects and shows how these domains interact with the phenomena discussed.
sources.note: The abstract (the only part reachable: benjamins.com is could not be reached by automated download, jbe-platform returns 404, no OA link in Crossref) is about the word/phrase-level domains of syllabification, syncope, epenthesis and consonant deletion in three Sudanese dialects; it does not mention word stress. 'Prosodic domains' here means prosodic-hierarchy levels, not accent. It is a condensation of chapters 3-5 of Ali's 2014 Toronto dissertation, whose separate stress section (2.3) is already held by the project and read.
